summary: Adds new GSS-API functions to ask about the attributes of security mechanisms and the mechanisms supporting them. The goal is to stop applications from hardcoding mechanism identifiers and instead pick one by what it can do.

eli5.summary: Instead of asking for a tool by its brand name, you ask for one that can do the job. This lets programs ask what each security tool can do before picking one.

questions: how to avoid hardcoding gss-api mechanism oids
subtitle: New GSS-API calls that let applications pick a security mechanism by what it can do instead of hardcoding its identifier.

tldr.problem: GSS-API applications have no way to ask what properties a security mechanism has, so many hardcode mechanism object identifiers (OIDs).
tldr.mechanism: Mechanism properties become attributes named by OIDs under 1.3.6.1.5.5.13, and three new optional functions find mechanisms by attributes, list a mechanism's attributes and describe an attribute.
tldr.outcome: Applications can select or exclude mechanisms by capability, and future mechanism specifications MUST list their attributes.

today: RFC 5587 is a Proposed Standard from July 2009. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Hardcoded OID Problem
sections.content:
The Generic Security Services API (GSS-API) lets applications use different security mechanisms, each named by an object identifier (OID). Because there was no API to inquire about a mechanism's properties, many applications had to hardcode OIDs. With new mechanisms likely to appear, that does not scale.

The RFC's example is Secure Shell version 2, which supports GSS-API mechanisms for authentication (RFC 4462) but prohibits SPNEGO (RFC 4178). Future mechanisms that negotiate other mechanisms would need to be forbidden too, yet an application has no way to list mechanisms and programmatically exclude any 'like SPNEGO'.
sections.eli5: Today a program has to know the exact name of each security tool. This RFC lets it ask what a tool can do instead.

sections.title: Mechanism Attributes and Attribute Sets
sections.content:
A mechanism attribute describes a feature of a mechanism or of a pseudo-mechanism, which is a mechanism that relies on other mechanisms to provide its service. SPNEGO is the example: without other mechanisms it is useless.

To keep the interfaces simple, attributes reuse the existing OID and OID set types. The RFC defines an open namespace of attributes as arcs under 1.3.6.1.5.5.13. Each mechanism has a set of attributes it supports, as described in its specification.
sections.eli5: An attribute is a label like 'waterproof' or 'has a zipper'. You can shop by labels without knowing the product name.

sections.title: The Known Attributes
sections.content:
Section 3.2 lists 27 attributes, numbered as arcs 1 to 27, with arc 28 onward reserved. They fall into a few groups.

  • Kind of mechanism: concrete, pseudo, composite, mechanism-negotiating (GSS_C_MA_MECH_NEGO), glue (the GSS-API itself) and not-a-mechanism.
  • Default use: GSS_C_MA_DEPRECATED and GSS_C_MA_NOT_DFLT_MECH both say the mechanism MUST NOT be used as a default.
  • Authentication: initiator-to-acceptor and acceptor-to-initiator, 'initial' authentication (passwords or keys on tokens) and anonymous names.
  • Per-message protection: integrity, confidentiality, MIC and wrap tokens, protection before the context is fully established, replay detection and out-of-sequence detection.
  • Other features: credential delegation, channel bindings, perfect forward security, compression and security context export/import.

The RFC then gives attribute sets for existing mechanisms. Kerberos V (RFC 1964) is concrete, offers mutual authentication, delegation, integrity, confidentiality and replay detection, among others, and its deprecated OID also carries GSS_C_MA_DEPRECATED. SPNEGO has just the negotiation and initial-token-framed attributes. SPKM attributes are left to a separate document.
sections.eli5: The list is a big checklist of things a security tool might do, like checking who you are, scrambling messages, or spotting copies of old messages.

sections.title: The Three New Functions
sections.content:
All three interfaces are OPTIONAL. Applications should use GSS_Indicate_mechs_by_attrs() instead of GSS_Indicate_mechs() wherever possible.

  • GSS_Indicate_mechs_by_attrs() takes three OID sets: desired_mech_attrs (the mechanisms MUST offer them), except_mech_attrs (they MUST NOT offer them) and critical_mech_attrs (they MUST understand them). It returns the matching mechanisms. With all three empty it behaves like GSS_Indicate_mechs() and returns every supported mechanism.
  • GSS_Inquire_attrs_for_mech() takes a mechanism OID and returns mech_attrs, the attributes it supports, and known_mech_attrs, the attributes its implementation knows about. It returns GSS_S_BAD_MECH for an unknown mechanism.
  • GSS_Display_mech_attr() takes an attribute OID and returns its name, a short description and a long description for humans.

A new major status, GSS_S_BAD_MECH_ATTR, reports an unknown attribute OID. In the C bindings it has routine error number 19, shifted by GSS_C_ROUTINE_ERROR_OFFSET. The C bindings also define new const typedefs, because the bindings in RFC 2744 apply const to pointer typedefs in a way that makes the pointer, not the pointed-to object, constant.
sections.eli5: One function says 'find me tools that can do X but not Y'. Another says 'what can this tool do?'. A third says 'explain this label in words'.

sections.title: Attribute Criticality
sections.content:
Attributes can be added at any time, and so can the attributes a mechanism supports. For example, a new attribute about contacting online infrastructure could be added, and Kerberos V would gain it without being modified. An application that relies on an attribute defined later cannot tell whether a given implementation knows about it.

The fix is the notion of critical attributes. An application lists the attributes it depends on as critical, and only mechanisms that understand them (meaning they know whether each is supported) are returned. The application can also ask which attributes a mechanism understands, through known_mech_attrs.
sections.eli5: If you really need a tool to be waterproof, you only want tools whose makers actually checked the question, not ones that never heard of it.

sections.title: Requirements, IANA and Security
sections.content:
All future GSS-API mechanism specifications MUST list the mechanism attributes associated with them. The GSS_C_MA_* symbol namespace is reserved for allocation by IETF Consensus, and IANA allocated the base OID as an arc of 1.3.6.1.5.5 and registered the values in Section 3.2.

The RFC says that being able to inquire about mechanism properties should improve security. Because attributes can be added at any time, developers must know which attributes their application depends on critically and MUST use the criticality features of these APIs. Each attribute's meaning may include a security component, and future protocols that use the GSS-API should refer to this document where it applies.
sections.eli5: New tools must come with a label list. And if your program really needs a certain feature, it should say so, so it does not get a tool that merely never mentions it.

items.title: desired_mech_attrs
items.text: Attributes the returned mechanisms MUST offer.

items.title: except_mech_attrs
items.text: Attributes the returned mechanisms MUST NOT offer.

items.title: critical_mech_attrs
items.text: Attributes the returned mechanisms MUST understand.

data.title: C prototypes
data.code:
OM_uint32 gss_indicate_mechs_by_attrs(
   OM_uint32         *minor_status,
   gss_const_OID_set  desired_mech_attrs,
   gss_const_OID_set  except_mech_attrs,
   gss_const_OID_set  critical_mech_attrs,
   gss_OID_set       *mechs);

OM_uint32 gss_inquire_attrs_for_mech(
   OM_uint32         *minor_status,
   gss_const_OID      mech,
   gss_OID_set       *mech_attrs,
   gss_OID_set       *known_mech_attrs);

OM_uint32 gss_display_mech_attr(
   OM_uint32         *minor_status,
   gss_const_OID      mech_attr,
   gss_buffer_t       name,
   gss_buffer_t       short_desc,
   gss_buffer_t       long_desc);
